title: A shipworm inspired the shield that dug the first tunnel under the Thames
body: Marc Isambard Brunel is said to have taken the idea from the shipworm, a mollusc whose efficiency at boring through timber he had watched in a shipyard: its hard shell protects the soft body as it eats forward. His tunnelling shield, patented with Lord Cochrane in 1818, was a cast-iron frame of three levels and twelve sections in which miners dug a little at a time while bricklayers built the permanent lining behind them, and jackscrews pushed the whole frame forward. From 1825 to 1843 Brunel and his son Isambard used it to dig the Thames Tunnel between Rotherhithe and Wapping, the **first tunnel known to have been built successfully under a navigable river**.

slides.alt: Side view of a tunnel. On the left, a finished brick-lined tunnel; in the middle, a tall iron shield divided into three levels of cells; on the right, the earth still to be dug. Yellow jackscrew arrows between the lining and the shield push it forward.
slides.caption: Miners dig inside the shield, jackscrews push it on, bricklayers line the tunnel behind.

slides.text: After opening, about two million people a year paid a penny to walk through. Since 2010 the tunnel has carried London Overground trains.

slides.question: What pushed Brunel’s shield forward as the miners dug?
slides.explanation: The cast-iron shield was moved forward by jackscrews, a little at a time, while shelves supported the earth until the brick lining was built behind it.

slides.heading: Match the name to the part it played
slides.explanation: Marc watched shipworms bore through timber in a shipyard; the shield’s iron frame protects the miners as the shell protects the worm.
